column11: CREST (Nature Medicine 2025;31:2806-2814, doi:10.1038/s41591-025-03738-z, PMC12353837): median duration of sasanlimab treatment 80.3 weeks (range 4.0-103.9) in Arm A, dosing capped at 25 four-weekly cycles (about 100 weeks), 46.3% completed all 25 cycles. Method: the book's R-DXD seed for a two-year capped course (lookup.py seed R-DXD: 1 / (1 + share on therapy after a year))
column12: Judgement. At a constant hazard from the median, 0.5^(52/80.3) = 63.8% are still on sasanlimab after a year and none after two, since the course ends at 25 cycles. The engine bills the stock (stock(t) = stock(t-1) x (1 - d) + new(t)), so each start earns 1/d patient-years; 1 + 0.638 = 1.638 patient-years per start gives d = 1 / 1.638 = 0.6104, the R-DXD seed's form. The constant hazard fits the trial: it predicts 43.7% still on drug at week 96 against 46.3% observed completing 25 cycles. The case for higher: the continuous mean exposure capped at 100 weeks is 1.29 years, which would give 0.776. The case for lower: none on this data; 0.362 (1 - 0.5^(52/80.3)) implies 2.77 patient-years per start, above the 1.92-year maximum the protocol allows. Most common reason for stopping was AEs (31.8% of Arm A).

column12: Judgement. No resubmission date is public. A resubmission in 2027 on longer CREST follow-up plus a standard review gives a 2028 approval, so 2029 is the first full year. column12: Above 1.0 on purpose, and flagged for the engine owner. The book's pool of 25,000 under this indication name is the BCG-unresponsive segment (TAR-200), a later line. Sasanlimab's label population, BCG-naive high-risk patients starting BCG, is about 31,000 a year, so it only fits as a multiple of that pool. The cleaner fix is to split the indication into BCG-naive and BCG-unresponsive pools. I did not do that because the brief forbids a second figure for one indication name. Also note that 31,000 is patients 'treated' in 2024, not new starts only. The case for a lower figure: some are on maintenance from a prior year, and the book's own CG Oncology figure is an 'up to' ceiling.

column11: Adjuvant nivolumab, the PD-1 add-on in curative-intent bladder cancer, reached 19% (12/63) of high-risk, nivolumab-eligible patients and 10% of all cystectomy patients in US community oncology practice ('Perioperative Treatment Patterns for Muscle-Invasive Bladder Cancer Patients Undergoing Radical Cystectomy in the Adjuvant Immunotherapy Era', PMC13304048; JCO 2025;43(5_suppl):704)
column12: Judgement on two counts. (1) The analogue: no PD-1 plus BCG launch has a measured uptake yet, since Imfinzi was approved only in May 2026. The closest measured precedent is a PD-1 added to curative bladder treatment with modest OS support, which is adjuvant nivolumab at about 19% of eligible patients. (2) The multiple is 0.5, because sasanlimab would reach market about 2.5 years behind Imfinzi with the same mechanism and design, the rule the mRNA flu seed applies to a second entrant. 0.19 x 0.5 = 0.095. The case for higher: a subcutaneous every-4-weeks dose suits urology practices better than IV infusion. The case for lower: regulators flagged added immune toxicity and more BCG interruptions.
